stories.headline: ‘National security first’: RSS-linked group demands Centre deny entry to Elon Musk's Starlink
stories.title: ‘National security first’: RSS-linked group demands Centre deny entry to Elon Musk's Starlink
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'national security' in title weight 70
article_sentences: The Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM), an affiliate of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), asks the Centre to block Starlink’s entry into India over national security concerns and Elon Musk’s public comments against Mukesh Ambani.

New Delhi: The Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM), an affiliate of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), on Tuesday called on the Union government to withhold permission for Elon Musk’s Starlink to launch commercial satellite broadband operations in India.
The group also strongly criticized "irresponsible" comments made by Musk targeting industrialist Mukesh Ambani and indirectly referencing the Indian government.

The developments follow Musk's intensified public criticism of Ambani on Saturday, where he shared media reports alleging that a Reliance-backed company aided social media campaigns for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and made substantial political contributions to the ruling party.

Earlier, Musk referred to Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani” on platform X, accusing him of maintaining a monopoly and blaming him for the administrative delays surrounding Starlink's satellite service rollout in the country.

While Reliance has refrained from making public comments on Musk’s allegations, the Centre maintained that India’s regulatory and authorisation system for telecommunications and satellite services remains “fair and non-discriminatory”, dismissing any claims of selective treatment as “baseless and misconceived”.
Ashwani Mahajan, SJM national co-convenor, asserted that India is fully justified in denying Starlink operating rights if the firm fails to resolve the country's national security considerations.

“The organisation is of the firm belief that blocking Starlink would send a message to trade partners like the US… that India is certainly within its rights to block Starlink based on its genuine national security concerns,” he stated.

Condemning Musk’s statements, Mahajan noted that while Starlink has applied for a commercial satellite broadband license, the application remains under review and has neither been approved nor rejected.

“It is unfortunate that instead of responding to clarifications sought from his company, on national security grounds, Elon Musk has chosen to make allegations on Indian businesses and the government indirectly,” Mahajan said.
He further suggested that Starlink might be attempting to bypass regulatory hurdles by influencing public opinion or that Musk’s reactions stem from difficulty in meeting statutory obligations.
“It appears that Starlink is perhaps not prepared to meet those specific requirements.

stories.headline: Delhi High Court directs responses in AITA governance and election dispute by November 6
stories.title: Delhi High Court directs responses in AITA governance and election dispute by November 6
stories.summary: In the hearing held on September 25, the order of which was released recently, the High Court said that rejoinders, if any, to AITA’s replies should be filed by November 6.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Delhi High Court has asked the All India Tennis Association (AITA) and the original petitioners led by former player Somdev Devvarman to file replies to the Court-appointed administrator Justice (retd.) Gita Mittal’s request to implead the AITA Trust and the Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA) in the ongoing proceedings to amend the AITA’s Constitution.

In the hearing held on September 25, the order of which was released recently, the Court said that rejoinders, if any, to AITA’s replies should be filed by November 6, the date when the matter will be heard again.
Justice Mittal, in her report dated September 14, had alleged large-scale financial misconduct and accused the office-bearers of stonewalling requests for documents and information.

The Court has also asked the AITA to respond to the request to produce the complete minutes of the Extraordinary General Meeting held on July 26 to ratify the new Constitution in line with the National Sports Governance Act, 2025.
The timeline for the conduct of fresh elections has been extended to November 27 from the previous deadline of September 30.

The AITA had requested the extension to complete the various mandatory administrative processes in the lead-up to the elections, chief among which is the finalisation of the 40-member strong Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) roster.

stories.headline: Chips will matter in the long term: N Chandrasekaran, Tata Sons chief
stories.title: Chips will matter in the long term: N Chandrasekaran, Tata Sons chief
stories.summary: Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran said that semiconductor chips are the future and will be required in the long run, irrespective of how soon India makes them, while speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi on Tuesday. Referring to Tata Sons' subsidiary Tata Electronics' attempt to manufacture chips for automotive, artificial intelligence (AI) applications and other uses, he added: "Whether we will get it right and hit the numbers in two years or three years is not the point. The point is chips are going to be fundamentally required." He said the company will continue to check on the demand and financial viability for the development, and it was difficult to have a clean spreadsheet in the current environment of uncertainty.Also Read: AI job anxiety comments are disaster marketing, says Nandan NilekaniWhile the world faces technology and fiscal disruptions, the way to progress would be to build resilient businesses that are derisked from dependence on a single geography, observed other industry experts who were part of a panel discussion with Chandrasekaran. “I continue to think technology probably is the biggest existential risk, but another risk is the lack of fiscal sustainability in Western governments,” said Jonathan Gray, president and chief operating officer at Blackstone. He added that emerging market countries were more responsible in many cases, and the moment of reckoning was playing out in the turbulent bond markets.While the current global environment offers governments around the world an opportunity to subsidise or incentivise resilience, one must be careful, said Rishi Sunak, former UK Prime Minister and member of parliament. “Politicians always like opportunities to protect local businesses. They like opportunities to put up barriers that protect the producers, and this gives them an excuse to do that,” he said.Also Read: Tata Sons chairman outlines three steps for sustained economic growthDrawing from his experience at G7, Sunak said the notion of derisking rather than decoupling, with “high fence for a small garden” floated by Jake Sullivan, then US National Security Advisor, captures the idea of prioritising national sovereign capability in critical sectors.Chandrasekaran said that while the world is still coming to terms with the tech disruption caused by AI, its impact in the long term is going to be powerful. He added that in a volatile environment, optimising for efficiency wasn’t the right approach, and neither was resilience opposed to efficiency. “To think that resilience is opposite of efficiency is a problem. I believe if you design it [systems] for resilience in an unpredictable environment, you're actually optimising for efficiency. You look at our business; we have seen supply chain disruptions across industries... Any disruption halts production,” he said. “It really surprises me how well we have done as a group with so many disruptions. We had an air crash. We had a cyber-attack. We had supply chain disruptions. Still, as a group, we will deliver the money, and margins are already done.”Gray said the firm wanted to continue to bet on electricity to power technology, data centres, autonomous vehicles, robots and other tech advancements. He added that AI will be moving from the desktop to the physical world, with self-reliant tech advancements taking precedence, such as defence and life science, where Blackstone plans on doubling down. “It will be good for India but the benefit to human health is going to be the number one thing coming out of it,” he said. “With new infrastructure in place, India will grow faster than any other major economy in the world and we are looking to deploy more capital in the geography for the next part of the century.”

stories.headline: Supreme Court plea seeks voter restoration route after Delhi roll revision
stories.title: Supreme Court plea seeks voter restoration route after Delhi roll revision
stories.summary: Supreme Court plea seeks voter restoration route after Delhi roll revision
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: A fresh plea in the Supreme Court seeks a separate route to restore Delhi voters dropped after the SIR exercise.
It argues that previously enrolled electors should not be forced to file first-time inclusion declarations.

A plea has been filed in the Supreme Court seeking directions to the Election Commission to create a suitable mechanism for the inclusion of voters in Delhi whose names were left out of the electoral roll after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), without requiring them to state that they are applying for inclusion for the first time.

The application also asks that previously enrolled voters should not be made to submit the declaration in Form 6 if it is "factually inapplicable" to them, and that a separate form or declaration should be prescribed for the inclusion of such voters.
Form 6 is the application through which an eligible person seeks inclusion in the electoral roll.

"The present application raises the issue arising from the mechanism prescribed for re-inclusion of previously enrolled electors whose names have been omitted from the electoral roll pursuant to the SIR in the NCT of Delhi," the plea said.

Filed through advocate Prashant Bhushan, the application also sought a direction to the Election Commission not to reject an otherwise maintainable claim for inclusion or restoration only because the applicant has not furnished the additional SIR declaration form.

While hearing the main petition on September 22, the Supreme Court had told the poll panel that notices under the SIR exercise in Delhi were going to people "almost mechanically" and that it should look for some additional safeguards.
The court had also said the basis for identifying a "logical discrepancy" required clarification.

The plea, filed by Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, also sought disclosure of the criteria, definitions, algorithmic parameters and operational guidelines used for classifying voters under the category of "logical discrepancies".

stories.headline: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afresh
stories.title: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afresh
stories.summary: Eli Lilly has a “follow-the-sun” model for its research and development wing, which gets 20 to 25 cents of every dollar from its sales revenue. Under this model, drug development never stops, with work on new drugs ticking round the clock across centres in the United States, Europe, and India.“Lilly has become the fastest developer of drugs in the world. One of the reasons for that is a follow-the-sun model. The work actually never stops on any pipeline product. We do it round the clock. It is like a baton passing every night, constantly,” David Ricks, the global pharmaceutical giant’s chair and CEO, told Forbes India in an interview while he was in New Delhi in early October.A globally recognised breeding ground for home-grown generics giants, India is hardly known to be a hub of new drug development. So, how critical is the country’s link in Lilly’s global chain?“India’s role is hugely important,” says Ricks. “It literally does one-third of the work. Every new medicine we launch has an Indian contribution.”Additionally, the India centre has developed new systems and processes that are shared with other centres and are being adopted globally. “In this, India is really a peer to our US and European centres, particularly for clinical trials,” says Ricks.Also Read: India is an important partner for Novo Nordisk’s R&D: Martin Holst LangeFat is the fuelEli Lilly has been in India for more than three decades. Ricks says this is the company’s fourth or fifth push in the country. Earlier efforts—including a 1993 partnership with Ranbaxy, once India’s largest pharma company which eventually passed into the hands of Sun Pharma, and launches in areas such as oncology and antibiotics—failed to gain enough traction. Lilly did not have products to reach large sections of the population.It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh. It is no longer merely a large market for cheaper, generic versions of the drugs MNCs spend billions to develop, or a country where they delay introducing their new drugs for as long as possible and then bear in stoic silence the loss of revenue as generic versions rush in.India is now also a hub of drug development for them and may become one of manufacturing as well. Lilly last year committed $1 billion to expand its contract manufacturing network here. Novo, the Danish pharma giant that competes with Lilly globally, shares its rival’s sentiments.“In the obesity space also, we have always had a very strong development presence in India,” Novo’s executive vice-president of R&D and chief scientific officer, Martin Hoist Lange, said in an interview with Forbes India in late September. “So, a good proportion of our clinical trials is with people from India. Thereby also obliging ourselves to launch our products in India and making our products available for people in India. So, from an R&D perspective, India is an integral part of how we do our development.”Lilly is setting up a joint laboratory with an Indian partner, whose name it has not yet disclosed, focused on process development work. At the same time, it is working with Indian manufacturers to produce registered starting materials and other key ingredients used in some of its biggest products, including its weight loss blockbuster Mounjaro. The move is part of a broader effort to diversify supply chains.“We have all become concerned that we were over relying on one country for these,” says Ricks. Establishing an Indian base for critical inputs, he adds, has become strategically important. About a year into the effort, “it is going really well”.For now, Lilly’s manufacturing footprint in India remains export-oriented. But that could change as the demand grows. “We tend to locate our manufacturing plants near our largest markets. So far, India has not been a large market. But as India grows, we’ll need to produce more, and we can look at production close to the market here,” says Ricks.Indeed, everyone likes to have their development and manufacturing bases as close to their largest markets as possible. That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs. The other factor, the unexpected catalyst, is artificial intelligence, or AI, which is changing the mechanics of pharma research.In a blog titled, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei says: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.”Also Read: The pill that could reshape India's weight-loss marketMight of weight lossIn March 2025, Eli Lilly launched Mounjaro in India. By October, it had become the country’s top‑selling drug by value overtaking the long‑standing market leader, GSK’s Augmentin. In June 2025, Novo entered the fray with Wegovy, its obesity‑focused semaglutide injection, and launched the much-awaited Ozempic in India in December.Both Ozempic and Mounjaro make you feel full sooner and for longer. But Mounjaro, which was approved five years after Ozempic and whose chemical name is tirzepatide, acts on both GLP-1 and GIP receptors. These are specialised proteins found on the surface of cells and play an important role in how the human body processes energy. Ozempic, whose chemical name is semaglutide, works only on GLP-1.India’s weight loss drugs category is estimated to have risen to ₹2,300 crore from ₹750 crore a year prior, largely driven by semaglutide going off patent on March 20, 2026, which saw 23 Indian generic versions of it launched within 24 hours.“It is inevitable,” says Ricks. “That is a by-product of our industry.” He however adds that the flood of generics has not affected Mounjaro’s growth. Instead, he says, “It has brought more people into the market.”These would be people inclined towards weight loss drugs but daunted by their high prices. “This is part of the normal cycle of our business,” he says. The same thing happened in Brazil and Canada.How does an inventor company convince buyers to pay more for their medicines despite the presence of cheaper generics?“Starting mostly with the physicians...,” says Ricks. “Through physicians we communicate… The clinical trials we have conducted… That if they are given a choice, what is the best alternative for people with obesity, people with diabetes… Now we have cardiovascular data that shows heart protection… And point out those differences when they are recommending something to a patient. I think we have comprehensive evidence versus semaglutide that is pretty convincing to most trained doctors.”Now everything in that market needs to be assessed all over again, because the next big thing is round the corner. The market that has so far been injectables is about to receive its first dose of pills.Beyond the needleOral GLP-1 pills are expected to come to India in the first half of 2027.“It is always helpful to be the first,” says Ricks. “But in the case of cardio metabolic health, it seems less important because these are chronic medications, and often the best one rises to the top. We saw that in the injectable market.”With the pills coming into the market, the fear is they will cannibalise injectables. There are use cases for both. Pills work well for patients who don’t want to inject themselves and those who prefer lower prices. Clinical studies by Eli Lilly show that in order to maintain a certain weight over time, patients can either lower the dose of Mounjaro or switch to Foundayo, which is Lilly’s oral GLP-1.The differentiation between Lilly and Novo’s products boils down to chemistry. Ricks says Mounjaro (tirzepatide) has achieved massive success partly because it mimics two hormones released by the gut after a meal, helping regulate appetite and blood sugar. Novo’s semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for obesity, works as a GLP-1 receptor. “The basic biology works a similar way. We have a lot of respect for our competitor,” says Ricks.Novo’s oral semaglutide is a peptide—a short chain of amino acids—which brings its own formulation challenges: Ensuring the drug survives digestion and is absorbed into the bloodstream.Lilly took a different approach with orforglipron (Foundayo), using a small chemical compound rather than a chain of amino acids (peptides) to activate the GLP-1 receptor. Ricks says this approach was more challenging scientifically but made production easier to scale up.Novo’s Lange did not reveal when his company’s weight loss pill will come to India, but emphasised that Wegovy was the only drug in the obesity space that had an established cardiovascular risk reduction, by 20 percent, and a liver risk reduction. “And those benefits are also seen with the Wegovy pill,” he said.He highlighted his drug’s benefits over its rival’s. “We have competitors that are in the subcutaneous space also give 21 percent weight loss at the highest dose. They don’t have the cardiovascular and liver benefits. They have a small molecule GLP-1 as a tablet. But that only gives 12 percent weight loss,” said Lange.The Wegovy pill has been launched first in the US where it has an 85 percent share of the weight loss tablet market. “And we are slowly but surely launching outside of the US. So far, we have launched in three countries outside of the US, with the next being Mexico,” he said.Also Read: Appetite for Ozempic wanesAfter weight lossBoth Lilly and Novo are betting on differentiated therapies as they expand their India portfolios.Beyond weight loss drugs, Lilly plans to bring medicines to India across therapies. But for that it must grapple with standards that are not the same as the international benchmarks for registration, including local data and local clinical trials. “Doing clinical trials in India is more complicated than other markets. So, we are working with the government to streamline that,” says Ricks.Dementia currently affects 8.8 million people in India, and it is expected to inflict 16.9 million by 2036. In May 2026, Eli Lilly launched its Alzheimer’s drug Kisunla (donanemab), also known as Lormalzi in India. It costs ₹91,688 for a 350-mg vial, which needs to be taken as an intravenous infusion once every four weeks.This, in a price sensitive market, is expensive, made even more so by the wafer-thin health insurance coverage in the country which translates into patients paying out of their own pockets. Lilly says all its medicines are priced as per the GDP per capita of a country. “While Kisunla and Mounjaro may still seem expensive relative to their generic alternatives, there is a pretty big discount relative to the European or US pricing,” says Ricks. “That’s how we fund our research and development.”Novo is excited about a new molecule called setagantide, which during Phase II trials showed 24 percent weight loss in 36 weeks and is now in Phase III. However, it too is awake to other opportunities in India. “From a commercial perspective, we intend to launch our products in India. It goes beyond obesity. In India, we are in diabetes, blood disorders, haemophilia, and sickle cell disease,” said Lange.AI-Powered R&DAmodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away. “That,” Ricks says, “is not the case.”Medicines live in the physical world. Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology. And it has to be safe. To prove a medicine’s efficacy and safety, it needs to be tested in people who have the disease. According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase.Also Read: Eli Lilly India Head on Mounjaro, Generics and the Future of GLP-1 DrugsLilly is deeply invested in AI for research and development, but in a different way.Making early-stage drug research more efficient is one. Drawing on data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects. These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.In September 2025, the company launched Lilly TuneLab. It is a collaborative artificial intelligence and machine learning drug discovery platform. This gives smaller biotech companies free access to AI tools that can help them identify promising drug candidates.Separately, Lilly has invested $1 billion with NVIDIA to build the largest biologic supercomputer in the world, called LillyPod. opening: Eli Lilly has a “follow-the-sun” model for its research and development wing, which gets 20 to 25 cents of every dollar from its sales revenue.
Under this model, drug development never stops, with work on new drugs ticking round the clock across centres in the United States, Europe, and India.
body: “Lilly has become the fastest developer of drugs in the world.
One of the reasons for that is a follow-the-sun model.
The work actually never stops on any pipeline product.
We do it round the clock.
It is like a baton passing every night, constantly,” David Ricks, the global pharmaceutical giant’s chair and CEO, told Forbes India in an interview while he was in New Delhi in early October.
A globally recognised breeding ground for home-grown generics giants, India is hardly known to be a hub of new drug development.
So, how critical is the country’s link in Lilly’s global chain?
“India’s role is hugely important,” says Ricks.
“It literally does one-third of the work.
Every new medicine we launch has an Indian contribution.” Additionally, the India centre has developed new systems and processes that are shared with other centres and are being adopted globally.
“In this, India is really a peer to our US and European centres, particularly for clinical trials,” says Ricks.
Fat is the fuelEli Lilly has been in India for more than three decades.
Ricks says this is the company’s fourth or fifth push in the country.

Earlier efforts—including a 1993 partnership with Ranbaxy, once India’s largest pharma company which eventually passed into the hands of Sun Pharma, and launches in areas such as oncology and antibiotics—failed to gain enough traction.
Lilly did not have products to reach large sections of the population.
It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh.

It is no longer merely a large market for cheaper, generic versions of the drugs MNCs spend billions to develop, or a country where they delay introducing their new drugs for as long as possible and then bear in stoic silence the loss of revenue as generic versions rush in.
India is now also a hub of drug development for them and may become one of manufacturing as well.
Lilly last year committed $1 billion to expand its contract manufacturing network here.
Novo, the Danish pharma giant that competes with Lilly globally, shares its rival’s sentiments.

“In the obesity space also, we have always had a very strong development presence in India,” Novo’s executive vice-president of R&D and chief scientific officer, Martin Hoist Lange, said in an interview with Forbes India in late September.
“So, a good proportion of our clinical trials is with people from India.
Thereby also obliging ourselves to launch our products in India and making our products available for people in India.

So, from an R&D perspective, India is an integral part of how we do our development.” Lilly is setting up a joint laboratory with an Indian partner, whose name it has not yet disclosed, focused on process development work.

At the same time, it is working with Indian manufacturers to produce registered starting materials and other key ingredients used in some of its biggest products, including its weight loss blockbuster Mounjaro.
The move is part of a broader effort to diversify supply chains.
“We have all become concerned that we were over relying on one country for these,” says Ricks.
Establishing an Indian base for critical inputs, he adds, has become strategically important.
About a year into the effort, “it is going really well”.
For now, Lilly’s manufacturing footprint in India remains export-oriented.
But that could change as the demand grows.
“We tend to locate our manufacturing plants near our largest markets.
So far, India has not been a large market.
But as India grows, we’ll need to produce more, and we can look at production close to the market here,” says Ricks.
Indeed, everyone likes to have their development and manufacturing bases as close to their largest markets as possible.
That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs.
The other factor, the unexpected catalyst, is artificial intelligence, or AI, which is changing the mechanics of pharma research.
In a blog titled, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei says: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.” Might of weight loss.
In March 2025, Eli Lilly launched Mounjaro in India.
By October, it had become the country’s top‑selling drug by value overtaking the long‑standing market leader, GSK’s Augmentin.
In June 2025, Novo entered the fray with Wegovy, its obesity‑focused semaglutide injection, and launched the much-awaited Ozempic in India in December.
Both Ozempic and Mounjaro make you feel full sooner and for longer.
But Mounjaro, which was approved five years after Ozempic and whose chemical name is tirzepatide, acts on both GLP-1 and GIP receptors.
These are specialised proteins found on the surface of cells and play an important role in how the human body processes energy.
Ozempic, whose chemical name is semaglutide, works only on GLP-1.

India’s weight loss drugs category is estimated to have risen to ₹2,300 crore from ₹750 crore a year prior, largely driven by semaglutide going off patent on March 20, 2026, which saw 23 Indian generic versions of it launched within 24 hours.
“It is inevitable,” says Ricks.
“That is a by-product of our industry.” He however adds that the flood of generics has not affected Mounjaro’s growth.
Instead, he says, “It has brought more people into the market.” These would be people inclined towards weight loss drugs but daunted by their high prices.
“This is part of the normal cycle of our business,” he says.
The same thing happened in Brazil and Canada.
How does an inventor company convince buyers to pay more for their medicines despite the presence of cheaper generics?
“Starting mostly with the physicians...,” says Ricks.

“Through physicians we communicate… The clinical trials we have conducted… That if they are given a choice, what is the best alternative for people with obesity, people with diabetes… Now we have cardiovascular data that shows heart protection… And point out those differences when they are recommending something to a patient.

I think we have comprehensive evidence versus semaglutide that is pretty convincing to most trained doctors.” Now everything in that market needs to be assessed all over again, because the next big thing is round the corner.
The market that has so far been injectables is about to receive its first dose of pills.
“It is always helpful to be the first,” says Ricks.
“But in the case of cardio metabolic health, it seems less important because these are chronic medications, and often the best one rises to the top.
We saw that in the injectable market.” With the pills coming into the market, the fear is they will cannibalise injectables.
There are use cases for both.
Pills work well for patients who don’t want to inject themselves and those who prefer lower prices.
Clinical studies by Eli Lilly show that in order to maintain a certain weight over time, patients can either lower the dose of Mounjaro or switch to Foundayo, which is Lilly’s oral GLP-1.
The differentiation between Lilly and Novo’s products boils down to chemistry.
Ricks says Mounjaro (tirzepatide) has achieved massive success partly because it mimics two hormones released by the gut after a meal, helping regulate appetite and blood sugar.
Novo’s semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for obesity, works as a GLP-1 receptor.
“The basic biology works a similar way.
We have a lot of respect for our competitor,” says Ricks.
Novo’s oral semaglutide is a peptide—a short chain of amino acids—which brings its own formulation challenges: Ensuring the drug survives digestion and is absorbed into the bloodstream.
Lilly took a different approach with orforglipron (Foundayo), using a small chemical compound rather than a chain of amino acids (peptides) to activate the GLP-1 receptor.
Ricks says this approach was more challenging scientifically but made production easier to scale up.

Novo’s Lange did not reveal when his company’s weight loss pill will come to India, but emphasised that Wegovy was the only drug in the obesity space that had an established cardiovascular risk reduction, by 20 percent, and a liver risk reduction.
“And those benefits are also seen with the Wegovy pill,” he said.
He highlighted his drug’s benefits over its rival’s.
They don’t have the cardiovascular and liver benefits.
They have a small molecule GLP-1 as a tablet.
“And we are slowly but surely launching outside of the US.
So far, we have launched in three countries outside of the US, with the next being Mexico,” he said.
After weight loss.
Both Lilly and Novo are betting on differentiated therapies as they expand their India portfolios.
Beyond weight loss drugs, Lilly plans to bring medicines to India across therapies.
But for that it must grapple with standards that are not the same as the international benchmarks for registration, including local data and local clinical trials.
“Doing clinical trials in India is more complicated than other markets.
So, we are working with the government to streamline that,” says Ricks.
Dementia currently affects 8.8 million people in India, and it is expected to inflict 16.9 million by 2036.
In May 2026, Eli Lilly launched its Alzheimer’s drug Kisunla (donanemab), also known as Lormalzi in India.
It costs ₹91,688 for a 350-mg vial, which needs to be taken as an intravenous infusion once every four weeks.
This, in a price sensitive market, is expensive, made even more so by the wafer-thin health insurance coverage in the country which translates into patients paying out of their own pockets.
Lilly says all its medicines are priced as per the GDP per capita of a country.
“While Kisunla and Mounjaro may still seem expensive relative to their generic alternatives, there is a pretty big discount relative to the European or US pricing,” says Ricks.
However, it too is awake to other opportunities in India.
“From a commercial perspective, we intend to launch our products in India.
It goes beyond obesity.
In India, we are in diabetes, blood disorders, haemophilia, and sickle cell disease,” said Lange.
AI-Powered R&DAmodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away.
“That,” Ricks says, “is not the case.” Medicines live in the physical world.
Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology.
And it has to be safe.
To prove a medicine’s efficacy and safety, it needs to be tested in people who have the disease.
According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase.
Lilly is deeply invested in AI for research and development, but in a different way.
Making early-stage drug research more efficient is one.
Drawing on data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects.
These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.
In September 2025, the company launched Lilly TuneLab.
It is a collaborative artificial intelligence and machine learning drug discovery platform.
This gives smaller biotech companies free access to AI tools that can help them identify promising drug candidates.
Separately, Lilly has invested $1 billion with NVIDIA to build the largest biologic supercomputer in the world, called LillyPod.
It is training AI models to predict human biology and eventually generate ideas for new drug programmes to help supercharge drug discovery.
“It will take years to fully train models useful to scientists,” says Ricks.
Novo, in April, announced a partnership with OpenAI and in September it partnered with Anthropic.
Both the partnerships are to embed advanced artificial intelligence across its entire drug development and operational pipeline.
“AI helps to amplify the volume and the speed, but it also helps by providing more insights and analysing the data that we generate.
In the clinical space, it is also a huge productivity gain,” says Lange.
Though AI can amplify and enable research, it cannot work in isolation.
“We still need the human insights on top or in parallel with what we do with AI,” he adds.

stories.title: Supreme Court asks Delhi governmente to seek inputs from IB on Hawara plea for transfer to Punjab jail
stories.summary: Bench takes a cautious approach, saying the case of Beant Singh murder convict is sensitive, and even the Punjab government seems to be reluctant
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) asked the Delhi government to seek inputs from the Intelligence Bureau (IB) on Beant Singh murder convict Jagtar Singh Hawara’s plea for transfer from Delhi’s Tihar jail to a prison in Punjab.
A Bench headed by Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale took a cautious approach, saying the case was sensitive, and even the Punjab government seemed to be reluctant.
“We know that every sinner has a future… Like how somebody said, if you kill a single person, you are a murderer.
Kill a few thousand, you are a conqueror… But we will have to look at the implications of the transfer on the society,” Justice Sundresh said.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Delhi government, informed the top court that Hawara was involved in a jailbreak and his death penalty was converted to life imprisonment in the murder case.
Contending that transfer might increase chances of his escape, Ms. Bhati referred to an advisory by the Ministry of Home Affairs on transfer of high-risk prisoners.
Senior advocate Colin Gonsalves, for Hawara, said he had personally visited his client in jail and found him completely reformed.
Ms. Bhati referred to a Punjab government affidavit which sounded apprehensive about the effect of Hawara’s shift on the law and order situation in the State.
Mr. Gonsalves submitted that the assassination of the Chief Minister happened in 1995 when his client was only 21 years old.
“His mother is very old, 82 years old and in serious condition.
He is only seeking a transfer to a Punjab high-security prison, and not seeking release.
He has a blemishless record in jail,” Mr. Gonsalves argued.

stories.headline: Delhi SIR : Plea In Supreme Court Challenges ECI Directive That Deleted Voters Must File Form 6 For Electoral Roll Registration
stories.title: Delhi SIR : Plea In Supreme Court Challenges ECI Directive That Deleted Voters Must File Form 6 For Electoral Roll Registration
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: A plea has been filed in the Supreme Court challenging the Election Commission of India's procedure in the Delhi Special Intensive Revision requiring voters, whose names have been deleted pursuant to the SIR exercise, to fill Form 6 to seek re-inclusion of their names on the voter list.

An interlocutory application petition has been filed by transparency Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri through Advocate Prashant Bhushan in the pending petition, where they have challenged procedures regarding a logical discrepancy in the Delhi SIR.
The petition has been filed through Advocate Prashant Bhushan and Neha Rathi.
They have pointed out that Form 6 requires every applicant to affirm that they are “applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the first time”.

It has stated that during the enumeration phase of the Special Intensive Revision(SIR) in Delhi, 47,56,722 electors (32.78% of the voters who existed prior to the start of SIR) were excluded from the Draft Electoral Roll under the category of ASDD (Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate).
For any person on the ASDD list, the only mechanism for filing a claim for having their name restored in the voter list is through Form 6.

The petitioners have pointed out that this creates a fundamental anomaly as all these people were previously enrolled on the voter list but are now required to submit Form 6 and make a declaration that they are seeking inclusion in the electoral roll for the first time, which is factually incorrect and wholly inapplicable to their circumstances.

Further, such persons would also become liable for facing punishment for giving a declaration under Section 31 of the RP Act, 1950 which provides for imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.

The petition also points out that the additional Declaration Form required to be submitted along with Forms 6 and 8, which has been prescribed through the SIR guidelines, is without the force of law and should be struck down.
Form 6 is prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, which have been framed under Section 28 of the RPA, 1950.

Section 28(1) empowers the Central Government, after consultation with the Election Commission, to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act by notification in the Official Gazette, while Section 28(3) requires such rules to be laid before both Houses of Parliament and permits Parliament to modify or annul the same.
However, no such procedure was followed for this additional declaration form.

stories.headline: Kerala Union Of Working Journalists Move Supreme Court Alleging Police Violence During Delhi Protests
stories.title: Kerala Union Of Working Journalists Move Supreme Court Alleging Police Violence During Delhi Protests
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Kerala Union of Working Journalists (KUWJ), Delhi Unit, has approached the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeking urgent intervention over the alleged unlawful detention, physical assault, manhandling and intimidation of working journalists covering student protests in Delhi on 10 and 11 October 2026.

The writ petition, filed through Dr. D. Dhanasumod, Secretary of KUWJ, Delhi Unit, raises serious concerns regarding the safety of journalists discharging their professional duties, the freedom of the press, and the alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution.
According to the petition, several accredited journalists covering the protests were allegedly targeted by personnel of the Delhi.
Police and the Central Armed.
Police Forces (CAPF) while documenting the events on the ground.

The journalists identified in the petition include Mr. Suhail Muhammed, Chief Reporter and news anchor of 24 News; Mr. V.S. Rahul, cameraperson of 24 News; Mr. Sajin, reporter of Asianet News and member of KUWJ; Ms. Roshni Rajan and Ms. Farsana, women journalists; Mr. Vishnuprasad, press photographer of Mathrubhumi; and Ms. Miji P. Jose, senior reporter of Manorama News.
The petition alleges that journalists were physically restrained, dragged away, manhandled, and detained despite displaying their press credentials.

It further alleges that some journalists were subjected to prolonged questioning and intrusive searches, while a photographer's camera was sought to be snatched and a woman journalist was physically assaulted while reporting live.
A particularly serious concern raised in the petition is the alleged disregard of the interim directions issued by the Supreme Court.

The petition refers to the order dated October 9 in Diary No. 63560/2026 and the subsequent order dated October, 11 in Contempt Petition (Civil) Diary No. 63801/2026 and Writ Petition (Criminal) Diary No. 63858/2026, the latter order expressly stated that “lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever.”

The petition contends that the alleged incidents warrant an independent examination of whether the actions of the police and security personnel were consistent with the Court's directions and the constitutional protections available to journalists.
The writ petition relies, inter alia, on photographic material and contemporaneous video recordings relating to the alleged incidents.

stories.headline: Supreme Court agrees to hear Trump administration's plea over Elon Musk's DOGE records
stories.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear Trump administration's plea over Elon Musk's DOGE records
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The US Supreme Court will examine whether Elon Musk's DOGE must disclose records under federal transparency law or qualifies for an exemption as a presidential advisory body.

The battle over transparency in the Trump administration has returned to the US Supreme Court, with the country's highest court agreeing to hear a dispute over public access to records linked to Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

The court's decision on Tuesday marks the second time it has intervened in a lawsuit filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), a watchdog group seeking documents related to DOGE's activities during the opening days of US President Donald Trump's second term.

At the heart of the dispute is a fundamental question: should DOGE be treated as a federal agency required to disclose records under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), or can it operate outside the law's disclosure requirements as an advisory body to the president?
CREW maintains that DOGE falls within the scope of FOIA and must provide access to the records sought by the organisation.
The Trump administration, however, argues that the department is exempt because it functions as a presidential advisory body.
The legal battle has already produced conflicting rulings.
US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in CREW's favour and directed the government to expedite the processing of its records request.
An appeals court panel also backed the watchdog's position.

The administration later challenged the appeals court's decision, arguing that the panel failed to follow the Supreme Court's earlier guidance on the separation of powers and interfered with the independence and confidentiality of presidential advisers.
This is not the first time the Supreme Court has stepped into the dispute.
In June 2025, its conservative majority narrowed the scope of a lower court order requiring the government to hand over DOGE-related records to CREW.

stories.headline: L Murugan Resigns As Union Minister, Says He Wants To Strengthen BJP In Tamil Nadu
stories.title: L Murugan Resigns As Union Minister, Says He Wants To Strengthen BJP In Tamil Nadu
stories.summary: Union Minister of State L Murugan has stepped down from the Union government and as a Rajya Sabha member, expressing his desire to dedicate more efforts to the BJP in Tamil Nadu prior to the Lok Sabha elections in 2029.
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'resigns as' in title weight 40

opening: Union Minister of State L Murugan has stepped down from the Union government and as a Rajya Sabha member, expressing his desire to dedicate more efforts to the BJP in Tamil Nadu prior to the Lok Sabha elections in 2029.

Sources said this was the request he had made to Prime Minister Narendra Modi -- to relieve him of his duties as Minister of State and Rajya Sabha MP, so he can dedicate himself full-time to strengthening the party from the grassroot level in Tamil Nadu.
